title: Is @FunctionalInterface mandatory, can a functional interface extend another non-functional interface, and can it have default and static methods while lambdas still work?

s1_definition.profdef: `@FunctionalInterface` is NOT mandatory — any interface with exactly one abstract method IS a functional interface regardless of the annotation. But the annotation is STRONGLY recommended because: (1) it documents intent ("this is designed for lambdas"), (2) the compiler enforces exactly one abstract method (accidentally adding a second → COMPILE ERROR). A functional interface CAN extend another interface, as long as the combined result still has exactly one abstract method. It CAN have unlimited `default` and `static` methods — only abstract methods count toward the SAM limit. Default methods enable composition (`and()`, `andThen()`), static methods provide factories (`Predicate.not()`, `Comparator.comparing()`).
s1_definition.analogy: The `@FunctionalInterface` stamp on a bank form is like "ISO Certified" — the form works without it, but the stamp guarantees quality control. If someone accidentally adds a second blank (abstract method), the quality inspector (compiler) catches it immediately. Without the stamp, the mistake silently passes and breaks things later when a customer tries to fill it in (lambda compilation fails far from the source).
s1_definition.oneliner: @FunctionalInterface = optional but recommended compile-time guard. CAN extend interfaces. CAN have unlimited default+static. Only ONE abstract method matters.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@FunctionalInterface` is NOT mandatory — any interface with exactly one abstract method IS a functional interface regardless of the annotation. But the annotation is STRONGLY recommended because: (1) it documents intent ("this is designed for lambdas"), (2) the compiler enforces exactly one abstract method (accidentally adding a second → COMPILE ERROR). A functional interface CAN extend another interface, as long as the combined result still has exactly one abstract method. It CAN have unlimited `default` and `static` methods — only abstract methods count toward the SAM limit. Default methods enable composition (`and()`, `andThen()`), static methods provide factories (`Predicate.not()`, `Comparator.comparing()`).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The `@FunctionalInterface` stamp on a bank form is like "ISO Certified" — the form works without it, but the stamp guarantees quality control. If someone accidentally adds a second blank (abstract method), the quality inspector (compiler) catches it immediately. Without the stamp, the mistake silently passes and breaks things later when a customer tries to fill it in (lambda compilation fails far from the source).

**One line to remember:** @FunctionalInterface = optional but recommended compile-time guard. CAN extend interfaces. CAN have unlimited default+static. Only ONE abstract method matters.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's brokerage fee calculation has multiple strategies: flat fee (Rs.20 per trade), percentage fee (0.1% of trade amount), and tiered fee (0.1% up to Rs.5 lakh, 0.05% above).** Each strategy was a separate class implementing `FeeCalculator`. Adding a "minimum Rs.20" rule required modifying ALL classes. The team refactors: `FeeCalculator` becomes a `@FunctionalInterface` with static factories for strategies and default methods for composition (withMinimum, withMaximum, withDiscount).

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Request: calculate fees for TRD-001 (RELIANCE, 100 × Rs.2450.50 = Rs.245,050).

**Step 2.** `FeeCalculator.percentageFee(0.001)` creates a lambda: `trade -> trade.getAmount().multiply(0.001)`. This is the ONE abstract method implemented.

**Step 3.** `.withMinimum(20)` calls the DEFAULT method which returns a NEW lambda that wraps the original: `trade -> { fee = original.calculate(trade); return fee < 20 ? 20 : fee; }`. The original lambda is captured in a closure.

**Step 4.** `.withMaximum(2500)` wraps AGAIN: another layer that caps at Rs.2500. Three lambdas chained.

**Step 5.** `composed.calculate(trade)` executes the chain: inner lambda calculates 0.1% = Rs.245.05, middle lambda checks minimum (245 > 20 — OK), outer lambda checks maximum (245 < 2500 — OK). Final: Rs.245.05.

**Step 6.** For small trade TRD-002 (Rs.4,208): 0.1% = Rs.4.21. Minimum check: 4.21 < 20 → returned Rs.20.
sections.s5c_hld:
**What is HLD?** The whole-system view. Here a custom functional interface (one abstract method, plus optional default and static helpers) is the plug point for pluggable fraud rules across the platform.

```
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    HLD — Pluggable Fraud Rule Engine (custom functional interface)
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
  │ UPI App     │  │ Net Banking  │  │ Card Switch  │  ← Client Layer
  └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────┘
         └────────────────┼─────────────────┘ HTTPS
                          ▼
                ┌──────────────────────┐
                │    API Gateway       │  ← JWT, rate limit
                └──────────┬───────────┘
                           ▼
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  FraudEngine (×5)                         │  ← Application Layer
         │  @FunctionalInterface FraudRule           │
         │   + check(Txn): Risk        (single SAM)  │
         │   + default and(FraudRule)  (compose)     │
         │   + static always(): Rule   (factory)     │
         │  rules supplied as lambdas at runtime     │
         └──────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                JDBC │                 │ Kafka (fraud.alert)
                     ▼                 ▼
         ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
         │ PostgreSQL       │  │ Kafka            │
         │ txns, rules      │  │ fraud.alert      │
         └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Observability: Prometheus, ELK, Jaeger           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The HLD insight: FraudRule is a functional interface with exactly one abstract method, so any rule can be passed as a lambda. The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation is optional (the compiler infers SAM either way), but adding it guards the contract — if someone accidentally adds a second abstract method, compilation fails before the bad build reaches production.
sections.s5d_lld:
**What is LLD?** Zoom into the FraudRule interface to show that @FunctionalInterface is optional, a functional interface MAY have default and static methods and MAY extend another interface (as long as it still has exactly one abstract method).

```
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
       LLD — Custom Functional Interface Rules (FAANG Level)
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy (SAM): FraudRule is a one-method strategy = a lambda    │
  │  Composite via default and()/or(): combine rules into one rule    │
  │  Static Factory: FraudRule.always()/never() prebuilt rules        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: each rule tests ONE condition                                 │
  │  O: new rule = new lambda, engine code unchanged                  │
  │  I: FraudRule has a single abstract method (true SAM interface)   │
  │  D: engine depends on FraudRule abstraction, not concrete rules   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<@FunctionalInterface>> FraudRule        │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────│
  │  + check(txn: Txn): Risk        1 ABSTRACT  │  ← the SAM
  │  + default and(other): FraudRule            │  allowed (compose)
  │  + default or(other): FraudRule             │  allowed
  │  + static always(): FraudRule               │  allowed (factory)
  │  + static never(): FraudRule                │  allowed
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     (can also: interface FraudRule extends BaseRule, if BaseRule
      adds no extra abstract method — still exactly one SAM)

  ── Facts the diagram encodes ──────────────────────────────
   • @FunctionalInterface is OPTIONAL (doc + compile guard only).
   • Default and static methods DO NOT count toward the SAM count.
   • A functional interface MAY extend another interface if the
     total abstract-method count stays at exactly one.
   • Object methods (equals/hashCode/toString) are NOT counted.

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. FraudRule highValue = txn -> txn.amount().compareTo(LIMIT)>0 ? HIGH : LOW;
  2. FraudRule foreign   = txn -> txn.isForeign() ? HIGH : LOW;
  3. FraudRule combined  = highValue.and(foreign);   default method
  4. engine.evaluate(txn Rajesh SAV2001 Rs.900,000)
  5.   → combined.check(txn)                          SAM invoked
  6.   → Risk.HIGH → publish fraud.alert to Kafka
```

The LLD answers the question precisely: `@FunctionalInterface` is not mandatory — any interface with a single abstract method is already functional and usable as a lambda target. The annotation only makes the compiler enforce the single-abstract-method rule. A functional interface can freely add default and static methods (they do not count toward SAM) and can extend another interface as long as the combined abstract-method count remains exactly one.
sections.s6_takeaway:
The FunctionalInterface annotation is not mandatory — any interface with exactly one abstract method is a functional interface and can be used with lambdas. However, the annotation is strongly recommended because it provides compile-time safety: if someone accidentally adds a second abstract method, the compiler immediately reports an error at the interface definition instead of at every lambda usage site across the codebase. This is the same principle as Override — technically optional but prevents subtle bugs.

In my brokerage fee service, the FeeCalculator functional interface has one abstract method (calculate), three default composition methods (withMinimum, withMaximum, withDiscount), and three static factory methods (flatFee, percentageFee, tieredFee). Each factory returns a lambda. Each default method wraps the current lambda in a new lambda that adds a rule. This creates a composable pipeline: `FeeCalculator.percentageFee(0.001).withMinimum(20).withMaximum(2500)` produces a fee calculator that computes 0.1% of the trade amount, ensures at least Rs.20, and caps at Rs.2500 — all from composing one-line lambdas without any class hierarchy.

A functional interface can extend another interface as long as the combined result still has exactly one abstract method. If the parent has an abstract method, the child must override it as a default method to keep the SAM count at one. This pattern is used by UnaryOperator extending Function and BinaryOperator extending BiFunction in the standard library. Default and static methods do not count toward the abstract method limit because they have implementations — the lambda only needs to implement the single abstract method.
